title: Zurich Completes Its £8.1 Billion Takeover of Beazley on October 1, 2026, Creating a Specialty Insurer Targeting About $15 Billion of Premiums
summary: Zurich Insurance Group's £8.1 billion acquisition of Lloyd's specialist Beazley became effective on October 1, 2026 after shareholder approval on April 22, regulatory clearances confirmed by September 14 and High Court sanction on September 22; shareholders receive 1,310 pence per share.
description:
Zurich Insurance Group now owns Beazley. Insurance Business reported that the Swiss insurer's £8.1 billion acquisition of the London-listed specialty insurer was completed on October 1, 2026, when the scheme of arrangement became effective after the court order was delivered to the Registrar of Companies. Beazley's shares were suspended that morning and were due to be delisted from the London Stock Exchange by 8am on October 2. Shareholders receive 1,310 pence per share in cash, with settlement due by October 15.

The deal's path was long. Zurich made a first approach in January 2026 at 1,230 pence per share, which Beazley rejected. A revised offer of 1,280 pence followed, and agreement was reached on March 2, 2026 at 1,310 pence. According to the completion report, that price was a premium of roughly 59.8% over Beazley's mid-January closing price of 820 pence. Earlier coverage of the offer described it as 1,335 pence per share, being 1,310 pence in cash plus a permitted dividend of 25 pence, and as a premium of about 62.8%; the two descriptions are consistent, because the higher figure includes the dividend. The total value was about £8.1 billion.

Approvals followed a standard sequence. Shareholders approved the transaction on April 22, 2026, with an earlier report indicating that 99.9% of the votes cast supported it. Zurich notified the European Commission on June 11, 2026, which started a Phase I review lasting up to 25 working days. The completion report says regulatory clearances were obtained across multiple jurisdictions, with all approvals confirmed by September 14, and that the High Court in London sanctioned the scheme on September 22. The reports reviewed did not name every regulator that cleared the deal. Earlier coverage listed the Prudential Regulation Authority, the Financial Conduct Authority, Lloyd's of London, Switzerland's FINMA and the European Commission as the approvals required, but the completion article does not confirm each one individually, and none of the reports reviewed mentions any Australian regulator.

Financing involved a mix of sources. Earlier coverage said Zurich would use about US$3 billion of existing cash, US$2.9 billion in new debt facilities and a US$5 billion capital raise completed in March 2026. The completion report says Zurich raised CHF 3.9 billion, about £3.5 billion, through a share issuance in March 2026 to part-fund the deal. The two figures are described in different currencies and may refer to the same raise at different exchange rates; they should not be added together. Zurich also held 4.50% of Beazley as of June 10, 2026, after purchases in the open market.

Governance changes have already begun. Nine Beazley directors stepped down, including chairman Clive Bannister. Five Zurich-nominated directors were appointed: Patrick Manley, Earl Randall Clouser, Helen Pickford, Kristof Terryn and Claudia Cordioli. Chief executive Adrian Cox is not among those departing, which suggests that operating leadership will continue through the transition. Beazley's syndicates and carriers will continue writing business, now inside Zurich's group.

Zurich's reasoning is about scale in specialty insurance. It says the combined business, headquartered in London, will generate about US$15 billion in specialty gross written premiums annually, compared with roughly US$9 billion today. Earlier reports said Zurich expects US$150 million in annual cost savings by 2029 and more than US$1 billion in incremental revenue opportunities in the medium term. The completion report says product overlap is limited and that Zurich expects revenue synergies from cross-selling through its global distribution network. At the announcement, Zurich chief executive Mario Greco said: "Together with Beazley, we will create the world's leading specialty underwriter."

Beazley's cyber franchise was central to the transaction. Its Full Spectrum Cyber product and its position in the Lloyd's market made it one of the leading writers of cyber insurance, a line that has grown quickly even as prices have fallen. Marsh reported this week that global cyber rates have fallen for 13 consecutive quarters, so the acquirer is buying into a competitive market, though the sources do not say what Zurich expects for cyber pricing.

For Beazley's policyholders and brokers, the immediate effect should be limited. Policies are written by its Lloyd's syndicates and insurance companies, which continue to operate. Over time, integration with Zurich could change underwriting appetite, capacity and systems, but the reports describe no immediate changes. For Beazley staff, the elimination of public-company costs and the combination with Zurich's operations may bring restructuring, although the source speaks only of cost savings targeted by 2029.

For the wider market, the transaction is a reminder that takeover premiums of nearly 60% are available for specialist underwriters, and that large insurers are using acquisitions to build specialty positions. PwC's review of US insurance deals notes that investors favour specialty carriers and MGAs, and that profitable P&C businesses attract buyers. It also removes one of the few large independent listed Lloyd's insurers from the London market, a point likely to prompt discussion about the future of the Lloyd's platform and of London's listed insurance sector.

Details that remain unknown include the final integration plan, any changes to Beazley's syndicates and the exact timing of cost savings. Readers should look to Zurich's results and investor updates for progress against the targets of US$150 million in savings and US$15 billion in specialty premiums.
source_name: Insurance Business (completion report, October 2026) and earlier Insurance Business coverage of the offer
image_alt: Corporate insurance merger and acquisition deal (illustrative)
key_points: Zurich completed its £8.1 billion acquisition of Beazley when the scheme became effective on October 1, 2026; Beazley shares were suspended that morning and delisted from the London Stock Exchange by 8am on October 2.
Shareholders receive 1,310 pence per share in cash, with settlement due by October 15; the offer was reported earlier as 1,335 pence including a permitted 25 pence dividend.
Shareholders approved the deal on April 22, 2026, regulatory clearances were confirmed by September 14 and London's High Court sanctioned the scheme on September 22.

Zurich's first approach in January 2026 at 1,230 pence was rejected, a revised 1,280 pence followed, and agreement came on March 2 at 1,310 pence, a premium of roughly 59.8% over the mid-January closing price of 820 pence.

The combined specialty business will be headquartered in London and targets about $15 billion of specialty gross written premiums, up from roughly $9 billion, with CEO Adrian Cox staying and five Zurich-nominated directors joining the board.
why_it_matters: Beazley is one of the largest underwriters at Lloyd's and a leader in cyber insurance. Its sale to Zurich is one of the biggest insurance takeovers of the year and shows how large insurers are paying high prices for specialty expertise.

title: ACA Marketplace Costs Jump in 2026 After Enhanced Subsidies Expire: Sign-Ups Fall Over 1 Million and Net Premiums Rise 58%, KFF Finds
summary: KFF's analysis shows 2026 ACA plan selections fell by more than 1 million to 23.1 million, average monthly net premiums rose 58% from $113 to $178, and enrollees shifted toward bronze plans with deductibles up 37%.
description:
The first year without the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies is showing up in enrollment, in premiums and in the type of coverage people choose. The enhanced premium tax credits, created by the American Rescue Plan Act in 2021 and extended through 2025 by the Inflation Reduction Act, expired at the end of 2025. This article draws on a May 19, 2026 analysis by KFF, a health policy research organisation, supplemented by KFF's earlier projections and reporting on 2026 benchmark premiums. An earlier version of this article combined several different figures, including a 114% increase and a 22 million count of subsidised enrollees, in ways the sources do not support, so the numbers below have been corrected and labelled as to what they measure. It is general information, not insurance or financial advice.

How much did premiums rise? Two different measures are often confused. The first is the sticker price of plans. According to figures reported by Becker's Payer Issues, citing KFF, the average increase in benchmark premiums, meaning the second-lowest-cost silver plan used to set subsidies, was 26% for 2026, with Arkansas at 69% and Alaska the only state with a decrease, at 1%. The second is what people actually pay after subsidies, known as the net premium. KFF's May 2026 analysis found that average monthly net premiums for all consumers rose 58%, from $113 to $178.

What happened to the 114% figure? In a September 30, 2025 issue brief, KFF estimated that average annual premium payments for subsidised enrollees would rise 114%, from $888 in 2025 to $1,904 in 2026, if the enhanced credits expired. That estimate assumed people kept the same plan, and the brief said it excluded state subsidies. KFF's later analysis says actual increases were smaller than that projection because many enrollees switched to bronze plans and because the groups facing the biggest increases left the market at higher rates. So the 114% was a projection for a particular group under particular assumptions, not an observed average.

How many people enrolled? KFF reports that plan selections fell by more than 1 million to 23.1 million, the sharpest single-year drop since the Marketplaces opened. Plan selections are not the same as people who pay and keep coverage. KFF cites Wakely, an actuarial firm, estimating that average monthly effectuated enrollment could be about 17.5 million in 2026, with a possible low of 16.5 million, compared with 22.3 million in 2025. Wakely's range implies a fall of 17% to 26% in individual market effectuated enrollment. The Congressional Budget Office projected average 2026 Marketplace enrollment of 16.9 million, a contraction of roughly 25%. Wakely estimated that about 86% of January 2026 individual market enrollees paid their first premium.

Who left? The decline was concentrated at both ends of the income scale. People with incomes of 400% to 500% of the federal poverty level made up 3% of 2025 sign-ups but 27% of the drop, with sign-ups down 44%, or more than 321,000. Combined with those above 500%, people above 400% of poverty were 7% of 2025 enrollment but 48% of the decline. They had lost access to any subsidy under the original law once the enhanced credits expired. At the other end, enrollment below 150% of poverty fell by about 441,000, or 4%, which was 37% of the decline. By age, enrollment among 18 to 34 year olds fell by 542,000, or 8%, from 6.7 million to 6.2 million, 46% of the total fall. Plan selections fell in 41 states, with the largest percentage drops in North Carolina (22%), Ohio (20%) and West Virginia (17%), while New Mexico rose 18%, which KFF links to a state programme that fully backfills lost federal assistance.

How did coverage change? Many people traded down. Bronze plans rose from 30% of selections (7.3 million) to 40% (9.2 million). Silver fell from 57% to 43%, a record low. Gold rose from 13% to 17%. The average deductible rose 37%, from $2,759 to $3,786, the steepest increase since 2014. KFF says that with the 2025 metal-level mix, the increase would have been about 6%, so the shift to lower-premium, higher-deductible plans accounts for most of the rise. The share of consumers in plans with cost-sharing reductions, which lower deductibles for lower-income buyers, fell to a record-low 37%.

What do surveys show? A KFF follow-up survey in late February to early March 2026 found that 9% of 2025 enrollees had become uninsured, 4% of returning enrollees had not paid their first premium, and 17% were not confident they could afford premiums for the full year. In California, a board report from April 16, 2026 showed cancellations among renewing consumers up by about 6 percentage points, with nearly one in five having terminated or been cancelled for non-payment by the end of March.

Is there a risk spiral? Analysts worry that if healthier people leave, the remaining pool becomes costlier and premiums rise further, which pushes more people out. The KFF material we reviewed documents who left and what plans people chose, but it does not conclude that a spiral is under way, and we cannot say how health costs among remaining enrollees have developed. Insurers will show that when they file 2027 rates, and readers should watch those filings and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services' effectuated enrollment reports.

What should consumers do? Compare the total cost, including premium, deductible and out-of-pocket maximum, not only the premium. Check whether a state offers subsidies. Remember that a bronze plan with a very high deductible can leave a household exposed to large bills. Consumers with questions about eligibility should use official marketplace tools or an independent navigator.

This article summarises published research and reporting and is not insurance, tax or financial advice.
image_alt: Health insurance marketplace and ACA coverage costs (illustrative)
key_points: The enhanced premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025; KFF's analysis, published May 19, 2026, reports plan selections down by over 1 million to 23.1 million, the sharpest one-year drop since the Marketplaces launched.

Average monthly net premiums for all consumers rose 58%, from $113 to $178; KFF's earlier 114% projection applied to subsidised enrollees keeping the same plan and was larger than the observed rise because many switched to cheaper plans.
Bronze plans rose from 30% to 40% of selections, silver fell to a record-low 43%, and the average deductible rose 37%, from $2,759 to $3,786.
Enrollees above 400% of the poverty level were 7% of 2025 enrollment but 48% of the decline, and the share receiving premium tax credits fell from 92% to 87%.
Wakely estimates average effectuated enrollment of about 17.5 million in 2026 versus 22.3 million in 2025, and the CBO projects 16.9 million; actual paid-up enrollment may be lower than sign-ups.
why_it_matters: Subsidy changes show up as lower enrollment, thinner coverage and higher deductibles rather than only higher bills. Insurers, employers and state regulators will watch whether the remaining risk pool becomes sicker and costlier.

title: UnitedHealthcare, Humana and Aetna Shrink Their Medicare Advantage Footprints for 2026 as Benefits Are Trimmed
summary: For 2026, UnitedHealthcare dropped one state and 109 counties, Humana three states and 194 counties, and Aetna one state and 100 counties, while analysts reported cuts to over-the-counter benefits and higher premiums for general-enrollment plans.
description:
The largest private Medicare insurers are shrinking where they sell and what they offer. Healthcare Dive reported on October 2, 2025, using plan data that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) released on October 1, that UnitedHealthcare, Humana and CVS Health's Aetna had all reduced their Medicare Advantage service areas for 2026. This article summarises that report and the analyses it cites. An earlier version of this article included an estimate that UnitedHealthcare was exiting plans serving roughly 600,000 members; the report we reviewed does not contain that figure, so it has been removed. The article is general information for readers and does not recommend any plan.

What is Medicare Advantage? Medicare Advantage is the privately run alternative to traditional Medicare in the United States. Insurers contract with the federal government and receive a payment for each enrolled senior, then offer plans that must cover what traditional Medicare covers and often add extras such as dental, vision or over-the-counter allowances. Plans commonly use provider networks and can differ in premiums, deductibles and out-of-pocket limits.

Which insurers pulled back? According to the report, UnitedHealthcare, the largest carrier, is offering plans in one fewer state and 109 fewer counties than a year earlier. Humana has the largest reduction of the three, with plans in three fewer states and 194 fewer counties. Aetna is exiting one state and 100 counties. Not every carrier retreated. Elevance Health added one state and 64 counties but exited the Part D prescription drug market entirely. Centene kept the same number of states and added 51 counties. Kaiser made no service-area changes, though it closed certain plans in the mid-Atlantic region and Washington state. Two smaller carriers, UCare of Minnesota and Samaritan Health Plans of Oregon, are leaving Medicare Advantage. Healthcare Dive estimates that hundreds of thousands, possibly more than one million, members may need new plans during open enrollment, which runs from October 15 to December 7.

What is happening to premiums? The report presents two views. CMS projects that the average monthly premium across all Medicare Advantage plans will fall from $16.40 to $14, a figure that includes group plans and special needs plans. However, for the general enrollment population, which Healthcare Dive says accounts for most of the programme, a Morgan Stanley analysis of CMS data found that enrollment-weighted premiums rise by $2.84 a month, or almost 22%. The difference comes from which plans are included and how they are weighted. A senior in an average county will have 41.9 plan choices in 2026, down from 42.8, according to an analysis by ATI Advisory.

How are benefits changing? According to a TD Cowen research note cited in the report, Aetna, Elevance and UnitedHealthcare cut over-the-counter allowances in non-special needs plans, and UnitedHealthcare and Humana cut them in special needs plans too. Analysts say insurers are raising deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums. Major carriers are prioritising health maintenance organisation plans, which have narrower networks and give insurers more control over medical costs, and are shifting broker commissions to steer enrollment toward more profitable plans. UnitedHealthcare said in a statement that its 2026 offerings preserve access to affordable Medicare Advantage plans despite programmatic funding cuts.

How big is the market? The six largest carriers, UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Aetna, Elevance, Kaiser and Centene, covered about 25.2 million seniors as of September 2025, almost three-quarters of Medicare Advantage enrollment. The report says the administration projects total enrollment to fall to 34 million from almost 35 million, which would be the first year-over-year decrease in roughly two decades. A projection is not an outcome, and final enrollment will be known only after the open enrollment period and CMS reports.

Why are insurers pulling back? The report links the retreat to government reimbursement pressures and rising medical costs, and to insurers' efforts to restore margins by leaving underperforming areas. Our reading of the report is that rural counties and less-profitable products are more exposed, but the source does not quantify this, so readers should not assume a particular county is affected.

What should seniors do? First, read the Annual Notice of Change that your plan must send before open enrollment. It will list changes to premiums, benefits, networks and drug coverage. Second, check that your doctors, hospitals and prescriptions are covered in the plan you choose, since networks and formularies change. Third, look at the out-of-pocket maximum, because a low premium can come with a high maximum if you need care. Fourth, if your plan is ending, you will normally be able to choose another plan or return to traditional Medicare, but the rules on supplemental coverage in traditional Medicare differ by state and by health status, so check before leaving a plan. Free counselling is available through State Health Insurance Assistance Programs.

What should investors and policymakers watch? For insurers, the questions are whether margin recovery offsets lost membership and how the 2027 payment notice from CMS affects plans. For policymakers, the question is whether plan exits leave gaps in rural areas. The report we reviewed does not answer these, and they depend on later data.

What are the limits of this summary? The service-area changes are counts of states and counties compared with 2025, and they do not tell us how many people live in those counties. The premium figures are averages, and a single plan can be very different. The benefit cuts are described by analysts across carriers, not by plan, so a specific plan's change must be checked in its own documents.

This article summarises a trade report and analyst commentary and is not insurance advice.
source_name: Healthcare Dive (CMS data, Morgan Stanley, ATI Advisory, TD Cowen)
image_alt: Medicare Advantage health insurance coverage for seniors (illustrative)
key_points: CMS released full 2026 plan data on October 1, 2025; UnitedHealthcare offers plans in one fewer state and 109 fewer counties, Humana in three fewer states and 194 fewer counties, and Aetna in one fewer state and 100 fewer counties.
Elevance added one state and 64 counties but left the Part D market entirely, Centene added 51 counties, and UCare of Minnesota and Samaritan Health Plans of Oregon are leaving Medicare Advantage.

CMS projects the average monthly premium across all MA plans to fall from $16.40 to $14, but a Morgan Stanley analysis found enrollment-weighted premiums for general-enrollment plans rising $2.84, almost 22%.
Aetna, Elevance and UnitedHealthcare cut over-the-counter allowances in non-special needs plans, and analysts report higher deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums and a shift toward HMOs.
The administration projects Medicare Advantage enrollment falling to 34 million from almost 35 million, which the report says would be the first annual decrease in about two decades.
why_it_matters: Millions of seniors must re-check their plans each open enrollment, and a plan that was affordable last year may have a different network or fewer benefits. Insurers are prioritising margins over membership growth.

title: US Property/Casualty Insurers Post a $15.8-$16.3 Billion Underwriting Gain in Q1 2026 as Combined Ratio Falls to About 92% and Premium Growth Slows
summary: Verisk and APCIA report a Q1 2026 underwriting gain of about $15.8 billion and a 92.4% combined ratio, while AM Best reports $16.3 billion and 92%; net written premium growth slowed to 2.9%.
description:
US property and casualty insurers started 2026 with their best underwriting result in years, but premium growth has slowed sharply. Verisk and the American Property Casualty Insurance Association (APCIA) reported on June 23, 2026, that the industry posted an underwriting gain of about $15.8 billion in the first quarter, compared with a loss of $864 million a year earlier. AM Best reports a gain of $16.3 billion. The two figures differ because the organisations use different data sets and methods, and this article gives each with its source. Claims that the result is the best in a decade could not be verified in the sources reviewed, so this article does not make them. The comparison below is with the first quarter of 2025, which was weighed down by the January 2025 California wildfires.

What do the Verisk and APCIA figures show? The combined ratio, which measures claims and expenses relative to premiums, was 92.4%, down from 99.2% a year earlier. A ratio below 100% means an underwriting profit. Net written premiums rose 2.9%, down from 6.8% in the first quarter of 2025, and net earned premiums rose 3.8%, down from 7.8%. The report says premium growth slowed sharply. Robert Gordon of APCIA is quoted as saying that net written premium growth slowed sharply to 2.9% in the first quarter of 2026. Incurred losses and loss adjustment expenses fell 9.6%, after rising 15.5% in the first quarter of 2025. Carriers returned $6.2 billion to policyholders in the form of dividends. Net income after taxes was $40.9 billion, up from $19.4 billion, and realised capital gains were $8.8 billion, up from $3.7 billion. Policyholders' surplus, the industry's capital cushion, was $1.24 trillion, up from $1.09 trillion. The figures are net of reinsurance, cover about 98% of US P&C business, and exclude state workers' compensation funds, residual markets, the National Flood Insurance Program and foreign insurers.

What does AM Best report? AM Best, using its own data, reports a net underwriting gain of $16.3 billion, against a $1 billion loss a year earlier. The combined ratio was 92%, a seven-point improvement. Excluding $10.9 billion of favourable reserve development, which is the release of money previously set aside for claims that turned out lower than expected, the accident-year combined ratio was 96.6%. Catastrophe losses fell to 4.2 points of the combined ratio, from an estimated 14.5 points a year earlier. Net earned premiums rose 3.9%, and incurred losses and loss adjustment expenses fell 9.3%. Policyholder dividends rose by $5 billion. Net investment income rose 10.3% and net realised capital gains rose 141.5%. Pre-tax operating income rose 97% to $39.5 billion, and net income rose 107.7% to $41.8 billion. Industry surplus grew 2.2% since year-end 2025 to $1.3 trillion.

What explains the improvement? Both sources point to the contrast with the first quarter of 2025. The Verisk report says that catastrophe activity was more stable than in the first quarter of 2025, when the Palisades and Eaton wildfires weighed on results. Verisk says personal auto drove much of the improvement, and that some carriers returned auto premiums to customers through dividends. Casualty lines remained under pressure. Neither report gives line-by-line dollar figures in the versions we reviewed. AM Best's adjusted measure is a useful reminder: without reserve releases, the underlying result was a combined ratio of 96.6%, still profitable but less impressive.

Why does slower premium growth matter? For several years, rate increases boosted premiums. Growth of 2.9% suggests that price increases are fading and, in some lines, turning into decreases. This matches other sources covered on this site: WTW's survey reports specialty rates falling back to 2020 levels, and Artex says US property buyers are enjoying their best market in years. In personal auto, the Verisk report suggests that insurers are returning premiums to policyholders.

What are the risks? One quarter is not a trend. First-quarter results can be affected by weather, reserve releases and investment gains, and the rest of the year includes the hurricane season. The fact that net income ($40.9 billion or $41.8 billion) was far above the underwriting gain shows how much came from investments and capital gains, which can fall as well as rise. Casualty insurers continue to face social inflation, a theme in the Artex and WTW reports.

What does it mean for customers? Strong profitability and capital can support lower prices and better terms through competition, but prices depend on the line, state and insurer. Customers should compare quotes at renewal and review coverage, not assume savings. It is also worth explaining why two organisations report different numbers. Verisk and APCIA use statutory data from Verisk's database for about 98% of the market, while AM Best uses its own compilation of industry statements. Differences in coverage, timing and treatment of certain items are common and do not mean that either is wrong. Readers comparing the two should look at the direction and size of the change, which is consistent: a swing from a small loss to a large gain, and a combined ratio of about 92%.

This article summarises industry reports and is not investment advice.
source_name: Verisk / APCIA and AM Best Q1 2026 industry results
image_alt: Property and casualty insurance industry financial analysis (illustrative)
key_points: Verisk and APCIA report a Q1 2026 underwriting gain of about $15.8 billion, against an $864 million loss a year earlier, and a combined ratio of 92.4% (99.2% in Q1 2025).
AM Best reports a $16.3 billion gain and a 92% combined ratio; excluding $10.9 billion of favourable reserve development, its accident-year combined ratio was 96.6%.
Net written premium growth slowed sharply to 2.9% from 6.8%, and net earned premiums rose 3.8%; incurred losses and LAE fell 9.6%.
Catastrophe losses fell to 4.2 points of the combined ratio from an estimated 14.5 points a year earlier, when the January 2025 California wildfires hit, per AM Best.
Carriers returned $6.2 billion to policyholders as dividends, and policyholders' surplus was $1.24 trillion (Verisk) or about $1.3 trillion (AM Best).
why_it_matters: Strong profits and slowing premium growth often come before softer pricing. For customers this may mean better terms in some lines, while casualty lines remain under pressure from claim costs.

title: IAG Invests in Sonder to Offer Policyholders 24/7 Mental Health and Safety Support During Floods, Cyclones and Other Major Events
summary: Insurance Australia Group, through its venture arm Firemark Ventures, made an undisclosed investment in Sonder, a round-the-clock mental health, medical and safety platform it plans to extend to customers of NRMA Insurance, CGU, WFI and ROLLiN' during major incidents.
description:
One of Australia's largest insurers is putting money behind a service that reaches customers before and during a disaster, not only after a claim. Insurance Business reported on June 15, 2026 that Insurance Australia Group (IAG), through its corporate venture arm Firemark Ventures, has made a strategic investment in Sonder, an Australian platform that provides mental health, medical and safety support around the clock. The amount of the investment was not disclosed. This article is based on that report and a follow-up announcement. An earlier version of this article described the move with an industry label and claims about its effect on claim severity that the sources do not make, so those statements have been removed. Nothing here is medical advice.

What is Sonder? According to the reports, Sonder offers round-the-clock access to mental health, medical and safety support through a single platform. Its clients have mostly been employers managing staff wellbeing. IAG already uses Sonder for its own workforce. Craig Cowdrey, Sonder's co-founder and chief executive, said the company's vision has always been to get the right support to people at the right time. A June 25 Insurance Business report describes Sonder as founded in 2017, with more than one million members as of October 2025, and quotes the company's own survey data in which 56% of members said they would not have sought help without it and 77% felt better after using it. Those are company figures and have not been independently checked.

What does IAG plan to do? The report says IAG intends to make Sonder available to policyholders during major incidents and extreme weather, such as floods or cyclones, so that help is offered while harm is still unfolding and not only after a claim is lodged. IAG's brands include NRMA Insurance, CGU, WFI and ROLLiN'. The article does not say which brands' customers will receive the service first, when it will start or who is eligible. Christine Stasi, IAG's group executive for people, performance and reputation, said the company wants to move beyond claims response to earlier intervention and prevention, and that earlier support in these moments can improve mental health outcomes. Scott Gunther, a general partner at Firemark Ventures, said the investment fits the fund's focus on technology that improves how risks are understood, prevented and managed.

What is the first rollout? On June 24, 2026, WFI Insurance announced a package for farming clients and their families across Australia, reported by Insurance Business on June 25. It includes app-based wellbeing guidance, confidential self-assessments, counselling and psychology support, and location-based alerts for severe weather such as floods and bushfires. The support is free for eligible WFI policyholders, though the article does not define eligibility further or explain how to enrol beyond the app. The report says it is the first reported use of Sonder for policyholders, and Sonder's chief operating officer Rob Deeming said early access to support can make a meaningful difference. WFI also cited figures on farmers' access to support and exposure to natural hazards that come from its own and others' research and have not been independently benchmarked, so we do not repeat them here.

Why is extreme weather a mental health issue? The NRMA Insurance and Lifeline Australia Extreme Weather and Suicidality Report, published in April 2026, was based on a national survey of more than 1,500 Australians. It found that 61% feel anxious about extreme weather, 53% said weather-related stress led them to make major life changes, and 42% said extreme weather concerns affect their daily lives. One in five Gen Z respondents changed career or job plans because of extreme weather concerns. NRMA Insurance chief executive Julie Batch said the impact of extreme weather goes beyond physical damage. NRMA Insurance has also worked with Lifeline to add disaster-resilience content to Lifeline's online support toolkit. These are survey results commissioned by the insurer with a charity, and they show perceptions and self-reported effects, not clinical outcomes.

Is this an insurance business? Insurers are used to paying for losses; they rarely provide a direct service to people in distress. Customers may value support that arrives with a flood warning or a cyclone watch, and the service might strengthen the relationship between insurer and customer. The sources do not claim that it will reduce claims costs, and no evidence has been published on that. Investors should be careful before assuming it will. A venture investment is also a small, early step for a large insurer, and the amount is undisclosed.

What questions remain? First, how data will be handled. Location-based alerts and confidential self-assessments involve sensitive information, and customers will want to know what IAG can see and how it is protected. Second, how success will be measured: uptake, satisfaction, wellbeing outcomes and any effect on claims. Third, whether the support reaches the people most affected, including those who are not digitally connected or who distrust their insurer. Fourth, how the service complements public emergency and mental health services rather than replacing them.

Where can people get help? Anyone in Australia who is distressed can contact Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call 000.

This article summarises company announcements and press reports and is not medical, insurance or investment advice.
source_name: Insurance Business Australia and IT Brief Australia
image_alt: Insurtech mental health and safety platform investment (illustrative)
key_points: Insurance Business reported on June 15, 2026 that Insurance Australia Group (IAG), through its corporate venture arm Firemark Ventures, made a strategic investment in Sonder; the amount was not disclosed.
Sonder offers round-the-clock mental health, medical and safety support through a single platform; its clients have mostly been employers, and IAG already uses it for its own staff.

IAG plans to make Sonder available to policyholders during major incidents and extreme weather such as floods or cyclones; the report names the NRMA Insurance, CGU, WFI and ROLLiN' brands but gives no launch date or eligibility rules.

An NRMA Insurance and Lifeline Australia report from April 2026, based on a survey of more than 1,500 Australians, found 61% felt anxious about extreme weather and 53% had made major life changes because of weather-related stress.

On June 24, 2026, IAG's WFI brand announced free 24/7 mental health and safety support for eligible farming policyholders and their families, which is the first reported use of Sonder for policyholders.
why_it_matters: Insurers usually act after a claim is lodged. Offering support while a disaster is unfolding is a different kind of service, but its effect on wellbeing and claim costs has not yet been measured publicly.

title: Moody's Flood Study: $375 Billion of Uninsured US Residential Losses in a 1-in-100-Year Flood, a 65% Protection Gap and Over $1 Trillion in the Extreme Case
summary: Moody's Ratings analysis using its RMS inland flood model finds that a 1-in-100-year flood could leave more than $375 billion of US residential losses uninsured, a protection gap of about 65%, rising to more than $1 trillion in a 1-in-500-year event and to about $472 billion by 2050 under an intermediate-emissions pathway.
description:
A large share of the damage from a severe US flood would fall on households and governments, not insurers, according to a Moody's Ratings assessment that has been reported in several forms since May. Reinsurance News first covered it on May 27, 2026, Risk & Insurance on June 9, and Insurance Journal on June 22. The assessment was written by Jennifer Chang, senior vice-president for sustainable finance credit, and Firas Saleh, director of North American flood models, and evaluates residential flood exposure across the country at the county level.

The headline number is for a 1-in-100-year flood, an event with a 1% chance of occurring in any given year. In that scenario, Moody's estimates that aggregate uninsured residential losses could exceed $375 billion, and that the nationwide protection gap, the share of the loss that is not covered by insurance, is about 65%. In a 1-in-500-year event, uninsured losses could exceed $1 trillion, with a gap above 70%. Looking forward, Moody's says that under an intermediate-emissions climate pathway the 1-in-100-year uninsured loss rises about 25% by 2050 to roughly $472 billion, and that high-exposure areas spread further, including into New Jersey.

The method is important to read correctly. Moody's used its RMS US Inland Flood HD model, which covers river, surface water and coastal flooding. It compared the replacement value of exposed homes with the value covered by the National Flood Insurance Program, and assumed that current insurance coverage and flood defences remain unchanged. The results therefore show structural exposure, in Moody's words, and are not projected realised losses. They do not predict a specific storm or year.

Most counties are not at the extreme. Moody's says roughly 90% of counties have some flood exposure, and in the 1-in-100-year scenario most face potential uninsured losses of $150 million or less. The concentration is in a small number of places: fewer than 2% of counties, spread across 11 states, hold 65% of the nation's uninsured exposure, each with potential losses above $1 billion according to Risk & Insurance. Counties with potential uninsured losses above $5 billion are mainly in Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina and Texas. In the 1-in-500-year scenario, counties above $5 billion extend to 11 states, including Pennsylvania and Illinois, and high-loss counties reach states beyond the traditional coastal hotspots. The protection gaps in these scenarios range from 45% to 75%.

The most vivid example is Asheville, North Carolina. During Hurricane Helene in September 2024, rainfall there exceeded the 1-in-1,000-year threshold, with one station recording 24.2 inches over three days, according to Risk & Insurance. Moody's RMS modelling indicates a protection gap of about 88% in Buncombe County across 1-in-100 to 1-in-500 events. Risk & Insurance added that Moody's revised Buncombe County's Aaa rating outlook to negative in March 2025 and back to stable in April 2026, a reminder that flood losses feed into credit assessments of local governments.

That link to public finance is the reason a credit rating agency is writing about flood insurance. Moody's says flood exposure is a growing credit issue for US state and local governments, driven by more frequent and severe weather, continued development in flood-prone areas and low insurance coverage. The fiscal effect depends on the absolute size of losses and on each county's or state's capacity to absorb them, which includes federal support, reserves, insurance payouts and governance frameworks, so the protection gap percentage alone does not capture it. Moody's concluded that flood risk is broadly distributed across the country but unevenly insured, and that many local governments face material potential uninsured losses that could strain their finances unless insurance take-up rises or resilience investment increases.

Why is the gap so large? Insurance Journal reported that the National Flood Insurance Program is the primary provider of residential flood insurance, and that private flood insurance makes up about 10% of the market. Risk & Insurance reported that take-up is low even in high-risk areas, at 10% to 30% along the Gulf Coast and Eastern Seaboard, that private policies have roughly doubled since 2020 without materially narrowing the gap, and that NFIP policy counts have fallen by a comparable amount to the rise in private policies. Mortgage rules also play a part. Federally regulated or backed lenders rely on FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area maps, which use a 1-in-100-year threshold to decide who must buy flood insurance. Moody's says these maps are mainly based on riverine flooding and do not fully capture extreme precipitation, greater storm surge or sea-level rise, which leaves exposure outside the mapped zones. The study warns against "relying solely on backward-looking statistics to characterize flood risk in a changing hydroclimate."

For households, the practical message is that standard homeowners cover does not pay for flood damage, and that being outside a mapped high-risk zone is not the same as being safe. A policy from the National Flood Insurance Program or a private insurer must be bought separately. For local governments and lenders, the study suggests that the question is not only the probability of a flood but how much of the loss would be left unfunded. For insurers, a persistent gap is both a risk and a market, because private flood has grown but has not closed it.

Limits should be kept in mind. The figures are scenarios built on a model and on assumptions about coverage and defences, they describe residential property only, and they do not say when a major event will occur. The reports also differ slightly in how they describe the concentration of exposure, so the original Moody's assessment is the source to consult for exact county-level numbers.

key_points: Moody's Ratings estimates that a 1-in-100-year flood could produce more than $375 billion of uninsured US residential losses, a nationwide protection gap of about 65%; a 1-in-500-year event could exceed $1 trillion with a gap above 70%.
Under an intermediate-emissions pathway, the 1-in-100-year uninsured loss rises about 25% by 2050 to roughly $472 billion, with high-exposure areas spreading further, including into New Jersey.

Fewer than 2% of counties, in 11 states, account for 65% of uninsured exposure, and counties in Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina and Texas each face more than $5 billion of potential uninsured loss; Buncombe County, North Carolina, home of Asheville, has a gap of about 88%.

The National Flood Insurance Program is the main residential provider; private policies are about 10% of policies in force, having roughly doubled since 2020 without materially narrowing the gap, and take-up is 10% to 30% in high-risk areas along the Gulf Coast and Eastern Seaboard.
Moody's says the results show structural exposure under current coverage and defences, not projected losses, and that the fiscal effect on a county or state depends on its capacity to absorb losses.
why_it_matters: Standard homeowners policies exclude flood, so a household that does not buy separate flood cover can lose its home with no insurance payout. At the scale Moody's describes, the gap is not only a family problem but a credit problem for local governments, which depend on property taxes and may have to fund recovery if homes are uninsured. The study also shows why mapped flood zones can mislead: lenders use maps that are mainly based on river flooding, while heavy rainfall and storm surge cause losses outside them. The numbers are scenarios, not forecasts, and they depend on assumptions about coverage and defences.
